strengths: Well-motivated approach to concept unlearning with clear identification of feature splitting as a limitation
Novel combination of supervised sparse autoencoders with explicit one-to-one concept-neuron mappings, enabling interpretable concept removal
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple metrics (UA, IRA, CRA) with systematic comparisons to 9+ baseline methods
Significant empirical improvements: 9.2% over SAEUiron baseline and 96.7% reduction in hyperparameter search cost
Thorough ablation studies validating each component and extensive appendices with additional analyses
Demonstrates practical scalability with 28.4% improvement on multi-concept (9-object) removal tasks
Strong evaluation of robustness to adversarial attacks and effectiveness on additional tasks (nudity unlearning, sequential removal)
Clear presentation with intuitive figures and well-organized methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing SAE techniques with straightforward supervised losses; core components (TopK SAEs, Pearson correlation) are established methods
Methodological concern: feature scoring in Eq. (4-5) uses all latent features rather than sparse-activated subset, contradicting the sparsity objective
Narrow evaluation scope: tested only on Stable Diffusion v1.5; generalization to other diffusion models and modalities unclear
Insufficient theoretical justification for why one-to-one mappings improve unlearning; feature splitting claim lacks rigorous proof of causality
Reproducibility issues: no code release mentioned, supervised label acquisition process vague, exact sample counts per concept not specified
Experimental limitations: UnlearnCanvas benchmark is relatively small (20 objects, 50 styles); SAEUiron baseline seems unusually weak; missing comparisons with recent concept editing methods
Evaluation methodology questions: classifier-dependent metrics (UA, IRA, CRA) without sensitivity analysis; missing false positive analysis for semantically related concepts
Limited failure case and edge case analysis: behavior with fine-grained concepts, maximum scalability with large concept sets, and concept entanglement scenarios unexplored
Hyperparameter sensitivity incompletely addressed: critical sparsity coefficient β shows large effects but limited selection strategy guidance
Decorrelation constraint computed on mini-batches may produce noisy gradient estimates; interaction between multiple loss terms (reconstruction, sparsity, concept assignment) lacks thorough analysis

strengths: Strong empirical results with 7.5% improvement in IRA over SOTA (SAELion 85.57% → 94.65%), demonstrating meaningful advancement on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark
Technically sound methodology combining TopK sparse autoencoders with novel concept-latent assignment and decorrelation losses that enable precise one-to-one concept-neuron mappings
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablations, qualitative results, computational efficiency analysis, adversarial robustness, sequential unlearning, and k-NN validation
Well-written paper with clear presentation and effective visualizations that convey complex concepts accessibly (especially Figures 1-2)
Addresses genuine practical concerns in model safety (NSFW content, copyrighted material removal) with demonstrated effectiveness and 96.67% reduction in hyperparameter search space
Extensive appendix with detailed ablations, standard deviations, additional visualizations, and systematic exploration of model variants
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope restricted primarily to UnlearnCanvas benchmark; generalization to other datasets, architectures beyond Stable Diffusion, or safety-critical concept removal scenarios remains unclear
Moderate originality - core contribution is applying existing sparse autoencoder techniques with custom loss functions to concept unlearning rather than fundamental technical innovation
Requires labeled concept data during training, representing significant practical limitation; paper lacks discussion of label acquisition at scale or handling of ambiguous concepts
Strong assumption that concepts decompose cleanly to individual latent units; failure modes and when this assumption breaks down are not thoroughly analyzed
Incomplete hyperparameter sensitivity analysis beyond λ coefficient (Section 6.10); interaction effects between loss components and their relative weighting deserve more exploration
Lacks analysis of failure cases; no discussion of when performance degrades or concepts don't decompose to single latents as assumed
Code availability not mentioned, limiting reproducibility; some implementation details (e.g., feature activation selection during training) could be clearer
Adversarial robustness evaluation limited to I2P benchmark; testing against diverse attack types would strengthen claims about robustness
Generalization to hierarchical/overlapping concepts, other modalities (text), or non-visual domains not addressed
Comparison primarily against SAELion using same SAE framework makes it difficult to isolate contribution of training objective vs architecture

strengths: Well-motivated supervised approach to address feature splitting through one-to-one concept-neuron mappings enforced via Concept Assignment and Decorrelation losses

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple dimensions: multiple metrics (UA, IRA, CRA, FID), thorough ablations, multiple application scenarios (sequential unlearning, adversarial robustness, nudity removal, style removal), and extensive qualitative visualizations
Significant quantitative improvements over SAEUron baseline: 96.67% on UnlearnCanvas vs. 82.29%, with 91.51% average object retention and consistent gains across all evaluation metrics
Interpretability and transparency advantages from explicit one-to-one concept-neuron mappings, valuable for safety auditing and accountability compared to unsupervised approaches
Rigorous feature centralization validation using K-NN classification experiments demonstrating that supervised training achieves claimed feature concentration
Robustness evaluation against both white-box and black-box adversarial attacks proving genuine unlearning rather than superficial suppression
Clear mathematical formulation with well-defined loss functions and comprehensive implementation details including hyperparameters, training procedures, and architectural choices
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations including closed-vocabulary constraints, scalability concerns, within-group concept interference, and architectural dependencies
weaknesses: Incremental contribution over very recent SAEUron baseline (Cywinski & Deja, 2025): while supervised adaptation is novel, the conceptual distance from prior work is limited and core ideas (SAEs, supervised learning, sparsity regularization) are well-established

Limited architectural scope with evaluation focused primarily on Stable Diffusion v1.5; brief SDXLTurbo results in appendix show different performance characteristics; no evaluation on newer models (FLUX, SD 3.0) limiting generalizability

Closed-vocabulary constraint requiring predefined concepts for supervision; unclear how method handles novel concept combinations or out-of-vocabulary concepts at inference time, limiting flexibility compared to some approaches

Incomplete scalability analysis: while 70 concepts tested, computational and performance scaling properties not thoroughly characterized; concept-per-latent design may face challenges with hundreds of concepts
Within-group concept interference incompletely resolved: semantically similar concepts still interfere; decorrelation constraint addresses macro-level interference but not fine-grained similarities

Hyperparameter sensitivity not fully characterized: grid search procedure appears ad-hoc with higher β values producing completely white images (compromising utility); limited analysis of critical performance-preservation trade-offs
No code release mentioned despite detailed methodology, limiting reproducibility and practical adoption by community

Dense methodology section (Section 3) with heavy mathematical notation that could better convey key intuitions before presenting equations; insufficient discussion of failure modes and patterns in unsuccessful concept removal

strengths: Well-motivated supervised approach to concept unlearning that addresses a real problem (feature splitting) in unsupervised SAE training with clear solutions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (UA, IRA, CRA, FID), diverse unlearning scenarios (objects, styles, sequential), adversarial robustness testing, and extensive ablations
Strong empirical results showing consistent improvements over SAEUron baseline (91.51% vs 87.16% on UnlearnCanvas, superior adversarial robustness at 57.50% vs 34.20%)
Rigorous validation of design choices through K-NN feature centralization experiments, uniform multiplier sensitivity analysis, and detailed loss component ablations
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, computational cost analysis, training details, standard deviations, and extensive additional experiments in appendices
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (scalability, closed vocabulary, within-group interference, applicability to newer models) without overconfidence
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (concept manipulation in Figure 1, qualitative results in Figures 6 and 10-12)
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work (SAEUron): the core components (SAEs, concept assignment, decorrelation) are not new; the contribution is primarily their supervised combination, which is incremental
Evaluation restricted to single benchmark (UnlearnCanvas) with limited assessment on newer diffusion models (only SDX-Turbo in appendix); unclear whether improvements generalize broadly

Fundamental scalability limitation acknowledged but not solved: one-concept-per-latent design tested only on 70 concepts, quadratic computation cost, closed-vocabulary constraint requiring retraining for novel concepts severely limits practical deployment

Insufficient theoretical justification for design choices: why TopK is critical, why specific loss weighting (β, λ, η) is optimal, and why Pearson correlation prevents within-group interference lack rigorous explanation
Incomplete failure mode analysis: within-group interference and concept blending (flames/jellyfish) mentioned but not systematically characterized; no clear guidance on when method succeeds/fails
Hyperparameter sensitivity: three loss hyperparameters require grid search with no principled approach for new domains; Figures 15-16 show performance varies significantly across multiplier ranges

Missing key experiments: no user studies validating concept erasure, limited analysis of semantically similar concepts, adversarial evaluation limited to gradient-based attacks, no systematic study of failure modes

Technical clarity issues: mechanism by which feature centralization (Eq. 5) ensures strict one-to-one mappings lacks formal analysis; auxiliary loss (Eq. 3) only uses largest k examples without justification; modified inference activation (Eq. 10) appears ad-hoc
Modest improvement magnitude: ~4-5 percentage point gains on primary metrics may not justify added complexity; 96.67% hyperparameter search improvement is difficult to interpret contextually
Ethical considerations underexplored: Impact Statement brief and doesn't address potential misuse (weaponizing to remove safety concepts, who controls what gets erased)
